newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu spars with rebel right-wingers.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu spars with rebel right-wingers.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu, having remapped the course of Israeli rightist politics by meeting Yasser Arafat, convened his cabinet on Friday after warning hawks to ride his peace train or risk getting thrown off.

Netanyahu took on hecklers and hardliners at a convention of his Likud party late on Thursday, recalling former prime minister Menachem Begin in a pugnacious defence of his government's handling of the peace process with the Palestinians.
"In battles for peace, as in battles in war, there is only one commander," Netanyahu told party leaders.

Netanyahu faced renewed criticism at a Friday meeting of the cabinet, still shaken by the stormy convention and internal opposition to Wednesday's meeting with Arafat, now Palestinian president but long denounced by the Likud as a "master terrorist".

"On the principle of continuing this (peace) process according to our understanding and in the way we are steering it, all cabinet ministers will have to accept it, or they won't be ministers," he told Israel Television on Thursday.

The Netanyahu convention address, in which the prime minister vowed never to budge from traditional Likud support of Jewish settlement and rejection of the Palestinian goal of an independent state, dismayed his PLO peace partners.

But his articles of rightist faith did little to blunt vocal opposition from high-profile ministers Ariel Sharon and Benjamin Begin -- son of the late prime minister -- and from Uzi Landau, head of parliament's Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee.

Referring to the election in which party chairman Netanyahu edged out Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres in May, and Wednesday's Arafat summit, Landau declared: "The Chairman of the Likud won, the Likud has been defeated."
Israeli media called Netanyahu's internal opposition "the Likud Intifada", an allusion to the Palestinian uprising against Israel of the late 1980s and early 1990s.
But most analysts said that for the present, Netanyahu retained overwhelming support of the Likud leadership, which acknowledges Israel's grassroots support of the peace process.
Israeli newspapers on Friday published opinion polls showing landslide support among Israelis for the summit.

In the cabinet meeting, Sharon again took up the anti-Netanyahu cudgel, charging the prime minister had refrained from carrying out vows to close PLO offices in Arab East Jerusalem and to rekindle a Jewish settlement boom frozen by the former Labour government, cabinet sources said.
Israel views Palestinian political activity in the city's Arab half as a challenge to its claims of sovereignty over the sector it captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
Both sides see East Jerusalem as their capital.

Following the cabinet meeting Netanyahu's office issued a statement saying that three Palestinian offices had been closed. "If any attempt is made to renew illegal activity, we will insist that it be stopped," the statement said.

A legislator of the rightist National Religious Party (NRP), a key coalition partner of the Likud, said on Friday his party would consider leaving the government if changes were not made in final plans for a long-delayed army pullout from Hebron.
Palestinians want the partial pullout from the West Bank flashpoint to proceed as agreed with the Peres government.
NRP's Abraham Stern said that among the needed changes would be a guarantee that Jews could settle in the town "forever".
